videoIdeas.title: The Prophet's Public Speaking Method
videoIdeas.hook: 1,400 years before anyone wrote a book on public speaking, the method was already there.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your post on Anas ibn Malik's narration (Slow. Clear. Three times.) already pulled 1,946 views with almost no push — it's one of your few pillar posts that landed. doctordaanish proves the 'save this, practical list' format prints views (91k on the 20s advice). Turn your best idea into a concrete, savable how-to.
videoIdeas.script:
Slow. Clear. Three times.

That's it. That's the method.

Anas ibn Malik said when the Prophet ﷺ spoke, he'd repeat a sentence three times so it was understood. When he greeted, he greeted three times.

Not because he lacked words. Because he understood something most speakers today don't: the point isn't what you said, it's what they kept.

You can have the best line in the room and lose it because you rushed through it like you were embarrassed to be heard.

Slow down. Say the one thing you want them to leave with. Then say it again.

People don't remember paragraphs. They remember a sentence you let breathe.

visuals.setting: Plain wall or bookshelf, mid-shot, you talking straight to camera, calm and deliberate energy — practise what you preach, speak slowly on camera.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'Slow. Clear. Three times.' appearing one word at a time with a beat between each, while you hold a deliberate pause before speaking.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open: say the first line, then freeze silent for 2 full seconds before the next word (demonstrates the method)
On-screen text punchline: 'The Prophet ﷺ was doing this 1,400 years ago' overlaid on an old book
Pattern interrupt: start mid-sentence 'say it again' then cut back to explain why

videoIdeas.title: What To Actually Do In Your 20s (Muslim Edition)
videoIdeas.hook: If you're a Muslim in your 20s, save this before you waste the decade.
videoIdeas.rationale: doctordaanish's 'if you're in your 20s pls save this' hit 91,710 views — the savable, numbered advice format is the single strongest thing in your competitor set right now and you have nothing like it. Put your blunt older-brother voice on it and you own a lane they're doing softly.
videoIdeas.script:
If you're a Muslim in your 20s, here's what nobody tells you straight.

One. Your network is being built right now whether you're trying or not. The people you sit with today are the people you'll be like in ten years. Choose them on purpose.

Two. Stop waiting to feel ready to speak. You learn to lead by being bad at it in a room, not by watching reels about it.

Three. Pick a skill the Ummah actually needs and get uncomfortably good at it. Vague ambition is just comfort with better branding.

Four. Your salah is the discipline everything else is built on. If you can't be consistent with the thing Allah obligated, don't be shocked when you're inconsistent with your goals.

You don't have time to figure this out at 30. Start now.

visuals.setting: Clean, slightly aspirational — walking outdoors or seated in a café/study space, smart casual. Direct, confident delivery, a little faster paced.
visuals.visualHook: Big on-screen text 'SAVE THIS' top of frame with a numbered counter 1–4 ticking as you talk.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: 'Nobody tells you this straight' said while pointing at camera
On-screen text punchline for point 4: 'the discipline everything is built on'
Cold open on the hardest line — 'vague ambition is just comfort with better branding' — then rewind to point 1

videoIdeas.title: You Can Pray And Still Need Help
videoIdeas.hook: You can pray and still need help. Both are true.
videoIdeas.rationale: lifeofdinoo_'s near-identical two-line post hit 51,763 views — the short, calm, 'two things can be true' format is working massively in this niche and demands almost no production. This is a gap for you: all your high performers are heated takes, you have no calm-reframe content.
videoIdeas.script:
You can pray and still need help.

Both are true.

Somewhere along the way we taught young Muslims that struggling means your iman is weak. That if you were really praying, you wouldn't be this tired, this anxious, this stuck.

That's not deen. That's pride wearing deen as a costume.

The Prophet ﷺ tied his camel and trusted Allah. He didn't tie it or trust — he did both. Tawakkul was never an excuse to refuse the means.

So make the dua. And book the appointment. Pray for ease. And ask the person who can actually help you.

Needing help isn't a crack in your faith. Refusing it out of ego might be.

visuals.setting: Quiet, intimate framing — closer to camera, softer light, lower energy than usual. Let it feel personal, not a lecture.
visuals.visualHook: Stark on-screen text 'You can pray AND still need help' on a plain background, held in silence for a beat before you speak.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on the reframe line 'that's pride wearing deen as a costume'
Camel/tie-it metaphor shown as on-screen text at the turn
End card with the two-line structure repeated as text for shares

videoIdeas.title: The Wall Between Deen And Career Is New
videoIdeas.hook: Ibn Sina would not understand the phrase 'secular job'.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your own post on this (Ibn Sina, al-Biruni, Ibn al-Nafis) got 1,732 views but zero comments — a strong idea delivered flat. The concept is a genuine gap-filler for your leadership pillar; rework it with a sharper provocation and a question that forces replies, like the ones driving comments on your political posts.
videoIdeas.script:
Ibn Sina would not understand the phrase 'secular job'.

Neither would al-Biruni. Neither would Ibn al-Nafis, who mapped the circulation of blood while memorising Quran.

To them, mastering medicine, astronomy, mathematics — that was worship. The knowledge was an act of drawing closer to the One who designed the thing they were studying.

We built the wall between deen and dunya much later. And most of us didn't choose it — we just inherited it and never questioned it.

So you clock out of your 'real life' at 9am and clock back in after Isha. Split in half for forty years.

What if your work was never supposed to be the break from your deen? What if it was supposed to be part of it?

Tell me the job you'd do differently if you actually believed that.

visuals.setting: Slightly more serious, intellectual tone — shelf of books or plain dark backdrop, smart shirt, measured delivery.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'secular job' with a red line striking through it as you say the first line.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: three scholars' names flash as text rapidly before you speak
On-screen punchline 'you inherited the wall, you didn't choose it'
End on the direct question as bold text to drive comments

videoIdeas.title: Stop Criticising The Brothers Building Something
videoIdeas.hook: Young Muslims are finally building their own spaces — and of course someone's mad about it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your 'third spaces' post (1,856 views) and your Surah Ali Imran 'encourage good, forbid evil' post both touch real community leadership but got buried under low comments. This angle combines your proven heat (calling out the critics, which drives your comment counts) with a genuine leadership message — building vs criticising.
videoIdeas.script:
Young British Muslims are building third spaces. Cafés. Study circles. Community hubs. Actual places to belong instead of a group chat.

And right on cue, someone online has a problem with it.

'It's not Islamic enough.' 'They're just doing it for clout.' 'Why isn't it in the masjid.'

Here's the thing. Allah called us the best community raised for mankind because we enjoin good — not because we snipe at every brother who actually tries to do some.

It is genuinely easier to write a paragraph tearing down someone's effort than to organise a single event yourself. One costs you nothing. The other costs you your weekend, your money, and your ego.

If you've got notes, build the better version. Nobody's stopping you.

Until then — let the people doing the work, work.

visuals.setting: Shot in or near an actual community space / café if possible, a bit more energy, movement in the background. Confident, slightly fed-up older-brother tone.
visuals.visualHook: B-roll of a busy café/study circle with on-screen text 'and someone's STILL mad about it'.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-rant: 'it is genuinely easier to tear it down than to organise one event'
On-screen text quote of Ali Imran 110 at the turn
Pattern interrupt: list the three criticisms as fast-cut text bubbles before answering them

videoIdeas.title: You Learn To Speak By Being Bad In The Room
videoIdeas.hook: You will never feel ready to speak. Stop waiting for it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Public speaking is your thinnest pillar despite being a stated niche — the Anas ibn Malik post is the only one that hit. This gives you a second public speaking asset in a blunt, actionable format that matches what's working (practical, direct, savable), filling an obvious content gap.
videoIdeas.script:
You're waiting to feel ready to speak. You never will. That's not the sign to wait — that's the job.

Every good speaker you've watched was bad in a room you weren't in. They stumbled, went red, forgot their point, and did it again the next week.

The nerves don't leave. You just get better at working while they're there.

So here's the fix, and it's not a mindset trick. Say yes to the small talk — the halaqa reminder, the two minutes at the youth event, the toast at your brother's walima. The low-stakes rooms are your training ground.

Ready is not a feeling you get before you speak. It's a thing you earn after speaking, badly, a hundred times.

Stop watching reels about confidence. Go be the worst speaker in a small room this week.

visuals.setting: Direct to camera, upright, a bit of intensity — this is a push, not a comfort. Plain backdrop, no distractions.
visuals.visualHook: Bold on-screen text 'You'll never feel ready' slamming on screen as you deliver the first line flat and unblinking.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: 'stop watching reels about confidence' — said while literally putting the phone down
On-screen punchline: 'ready is earned AFTER, not felt BEFORE'
Cold open on the challenge: 'go be the worst speaker in a small room this week'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best engagement post by far — 208 likes and 8,579 views. The hook ('Can't believe we're still discussing the necessity of protests in 2026') leads with exasperation and a timestamp, which creates instant stance and timeliness. People like and share posts that voice a frustration they already feel. This is your proven formula: a clear, slightly fed-up opinion stated as fact.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The caption gets cut off and the second half rambles into a vague swipe ('probably use it to make themselves bett...'). With this many eyes on it, you left reach on the table by not ending on a sharp question to convert that attention into comments — it only got 12 despite 208 likes. Close with one direct prompt.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your highest view count (8,613). The caption draws a clean historical parallel — Iraq/Afghanistan then Iran, 'same guise' — which is exactly your strength: you compress a political point into a tight, repeatable structure. The parallelism ('same people', 'same guise') is memorable and makes people stop.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 24 comments on 8,613 views is decent but the ratio shows it provoked agreement, not conversation. This topic is high-risk/high-reach; the lesson for your pillars is to steal this exact 'then vs now, same pattern' structure for leadership and mindset content (e.g. the deen/career wall) where you can own the conversation without relying on news cycles you can't control.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 3,397 views and 100 likes — your strongest-performing actual self-development post. 'New model every September. Same habits every morning' is a genuinely good hook: tight, aphoristic, and it reframes self-improvement against tech culture. You also asked a question ('What's the last thing you upgraded in yourself?'), which is the right instinct.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 4 comments despite a direct question — the question came after the caption got long and credited '@...', burying it. Put the question earlier and make it easier to answer in two words. Also this proves your mindset content CAN travel; lean into this aphorism-first style more often instead of reserving your best hooks for political posts.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 'Slow. Clear. Three times.' is the single best hook in your public speaking pillar — three fragments, concrete, mysterious enough to make people watch to understand it. Grounding it in Anas ibn Malik's narration gives it authority competitors' generic speaking tips lack. 1,946 views with no controversy is a strong organic signal.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 3 comments. The question ('What's the one line you want people to leave your next talk with?') is good but abstract for people who don't give talks — reframe it so a non-speaker can answer (e.g. 'what's a sentence someone said once that you still remember?'). This idea deserves a re-make as a full savable how-to; it's underselling a top concept.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 1,732 views on a genuinely original idea — the deen/career divide as an inherited, modern invention. The 'Ibn Sina, al-Biruni and Ibn al-Nafis would not understand the phrase secular job' line is a strong, specific, intellectually confident hook that fits your older-brother voice perfectly.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments — the post states a point and stops. There's no tension and no ask, so there's nothing to reply to. Your political posts get comments because they take a side against someone; apply that here by adding friction ('most of us just inherited this wall and never questioned it — tell me the job you'd do differently if you believed that'). A great idea delivered flat.
